name: Король позаду пішака
description:
We have just seen again when mating with the rook that the king is an important contributor. Without the help of our own king we cannot get the job done. In the endgame with king and pawn against king the king also plays a crucial role. From the Promotionmonster lessons you may remember the techniques of shouldering and support. With 'shouldering' we place our own king in such a way that the opponent's king cannot reach the promotion square (see example 1). With 'supporting' we cover our own pawn and, if possible, make sure that the opponent's king cannot occupy the promotion square (see example 2). In both cases we succeed in getting the pawn promoted.

But what if the other player's king can occupy the promotion square? We will talk about that in the coming lessons. In this lesson we will look at positions in which our king is next to or just behind our own pawn and the opponent's king is just in front of it.

In examples 3 and 4 we see an important endgame theme emerge that we also saw in the checkmate with the rook: zugzwang! Here we see that the result depends on whose move it is. Example 3 and 4 are the same BUT: if it is black's move, white wins and if it is white's move, black holds a draw.

In examples 5 and 6 we use the knowledge from examples 3 and 4 and learn a new concept: opposition!

In Example 7 we see that if the king stands on or next to the promotion square, the defender always holds a draw in case of an edge pawn.

What do you have to do?

Is it your turn and you only have a king? Then make a draw. Is it your turn and you have a pawn? Then go for the win. In either case, try to use opposition.

examples.text: The white king shoulders the black king.
The white king supports the pawn and in the process also controls the promotion square.

If black were not obliged to make a move here, he/she could never lose the game. Unfortunately, he/she is on the move here and is in zugzwang. The only move is 1...Kf7 after which white can continue to support the pawn with 2.Kd7, ensuring that the black king can no longer occupy the promotion square. On the next move white promotes.

White would like to pass the turn to black (see the previous example), but of course skipping a move is not allowed. The only way to keep covering the pawn is with 1.Ke6, but then black is stalemated! If White lets go of the pawn, then of course Black captures the pawn and it is a draw because with only a king you can never mate the other (later in the lesson on insufficient material you will learn that more positions are theoretically drawn).

It's black's move, but there is an important difference from Example 3. The black king can now move to an additional square. However, it is very important which square he chooses. Black must move to the promotion square in order to move the king opposite the other king one move later: 1...Ke8 2.Kd6 Kd8. This is also called opposition. The kings are on the same file with an odd number of squares between them. The player not on the move has opposition. If white advances the pawn with 3.e7+, then black plays 3...Ke8 and we reach example 4. Black holds a draw!

If black plays the king to d8 in example 5, we end up in this example. After 1.Kd6 it is White who has opposition! 1…Ke8 2.e7 and we know this position from example 3. Black is forced to move: 2…Kf7 3.Kd7 and White promotes.

If white plays 1.h7, black is stalemate. Square i7 does not exist, so the black king cannot make a move (compare this with example 3 where the black king can move diagonally forward). If White does not advance the pawn, Black will continue to play the king back and forth between squares g8, h8 and h7. White cannot progress any further.
